intro: To turn on Mail Privacy Protection in Apple Mail on Mac, open Mail, choose Mail > Settings, click Privacy, and select Protect Mail Activity. That hides your IP address from senders and downloads remote content in the background.
tldr: Open Mail, choose Mail > Settings, click Privacy, then select Protect Mail Activity.
Protect Mail Activity hides your IP address from senders and downloads remote content in the background.
Keep Hide IP Address selected. Apple selects it for you when Protect Mail Activity is on.
If the setting seems to fail, check the network setting that limits IP address tracking for your Wi-Fi or Ethernet.
On iCloud.com, use the Settings button, then Privacy & Security, then check Protect Mail Activity.

blocks.text: Where Mail Privacy Protection lives in Apple Mail

Mail Privacy Protection is a setting inside the Mail app. You don't download anything extra, and you don't need System Settings. Apple's help page title uses the longer name, Mail Privacy Protection. The checkbox you actually select says Protect Mail Activity, so look for that label.

Before you start, make sure Mail is the front app. The Mail menu only shows in the menu bar when Mail is active. If you're in Finder or Safari, click a Mail window first. Then follow the steps above in order, because each one depends on the one before it.
What the three Privacy options do on Mac
Apple's Change Privacy settings page lists three options on a Mac. They work together, but each one covers a different gap. Here is what Apple says about each.

items: Protect Mail Activity hides your IP address from senders. It also downloads remote content in the background.
Hide IP Address is selected automatically when Protect Mail Activity is on. Apple recommends keeping it selected if you turn Protect Mail Activity off.
Block All Remote Content is what Apple recommends if you turn Protect Mail Activity off.

blocks.text: For most people, the first two options are the right pair. Keep Protect Mail Activity on, and leave Hide IP Address selected. Block All Remote Content is a different trade-off. Remote content, such as images, stops loading by default, so some messages look plainer than the sender intended.
Why hiding your IP address matters

Your IP address points to your network and a rough location. When a message loads a remote image, Mail asks a server for that file. That request carries your IP address. Apple says Protect Mail Activity hides it from senders.

Apple's legal page adds detail. Remote content goes through two relays run by different entities. Apple says the setting downloads remote content in the background by default in Mail and on iCloud.com. Read that as a description, not a promise that every tracker is blocked.

Here is a worked example. Say a newsletter has a small image at the bottom. With Protect Mail Activity on, Mail fetches that image through Apple's relays. The sender's server then sees a relay address rather than your own network address. The newsletter itself looks the same to you.
Who should keep Mail Privacy Protection on

Keep it on if you don't want senders learning your IP address from messages you open. It suits anyone who reads mail on a laptop that moves between networks, such as home, office, and public Wi-Fi. If one message won't show properly, change the setting for a short test, then put it back. Don't leave privacy off for good because of a single message.
Check that all three options are set

After the steps, the Privacy pane is your check. Apple's pages don't describe another place to confirm the status. Look at Protect Mail Activity and Hide IP Address first. Block All Remote Content matters when Protect Mail Activity is off, because Apple recommends it in that case.
Open rates and what the numbers show

Email senders noticed the change first. Litmus's market share page says Apple accounts for 76.56% of tracked email opens for September 2026. That figure is based on over 1.5 billion tracked opens. A lemlist article cites 64.66% for May 2026 from a Litmus report. The two numbers conflict, so cite the Litmus page and its date.

Older data points the same way. Omeda's client data shows its total open rate rose from 22.6% in May to July 2021 to 40.5% in February and March 2022. Click rates stayed about 2.4%. Omeda's numbers come from its own clients and are not peer reviewed.

For you as the reader, the lesson is simple. A sender may count an open that happened in the background. Whether you read the message is a separate question. Treat open rates as noisy, not as a measure of who read what.
Mail Privacy Protection on iCloud.com
If you read mail at icloud.com, the setting sits under a different menu. The labels differ from the Mac app. Use this path.

items: Go to icloud.com/mail and sign in.
Click the Settings button above the Mailboxes list.
Select Privacy & Security in the sidebar.

blocks.text: Apple says this feature is not available in all countries or regions. If you don't see the option, your region may not offer it. Apple's page also doesn't say which browsers are supported, so test in the browser you use most.
Fixing the 'Your network preferences prevent content from loading privately' error

A thread on Apple Community, started in October 2021 about Monterey, reports this error with Protect Mail Activity on. Posters offered three fixes. Apple did not confirm them, so treat them as community suggestions.

items: Turn off Limit IP Address Tracking for the Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection you use.
Turn off the web shield in third-party antivirus software.

blocks.text: The first fix needs care. Apple says that if the network setting that limits IP address tracking is off for Wi-Fi or Ethernet, your IP address is not hidden on that network. So turning it off undoes the protection you just set. The thread doesn't discuss that trade-off.

Start with the least risky step. Check which connection you're on, then read Apple's network note before you change anything. If you turn a setting off to test, switch it back on once you know the cause.
Common mistakes with Protect Mail Activity

items: Expecting every tracker to disappear. Apple describes hiding your IP address and downloading remote content in the background. It does not promise to stop everything.
Turning off Hide IP Address while Protect Mail Activity is also off. Apple recommends keeping it selected in that case.
Forgetting the network setting. If it is off on your current Wi-Fi or Ethernet, your IP stays visible on that network.
Searching for a keyboard shortcut. The Apple pages I checked list none for this setting, so use the menu path.
Assuming the Mac and iCloud.com labels match. The iCloud path uses Privacy & Security in the sidebar.

blocks.text: What changed in macOS 27 Golden Gate

9to5Mac reported that macOS 27 Golden Gate launches September 14, 2026. Apple's Mail What's new page lists Suggestions, Personalized Writing, and Expanded Search Results. It does not mention Protect Mail Activity, Hide IP Address, or Block All Remote Content.

I did not find a change to the privacy setting in macOS 27. Apple's macOS 27 page still showed beta-style wording when I checked, so it is not a clean source for the release date. Apple's Mail pages also don't name a macOS version for these steps. If your Privacy pane looks different, follow what you see and check Apple's current Mail help.
Turn it off, or switch to Block All Remote Content

To turn Protect Mail Activity off, go back to Mail > Settings > Privacy and clear the Protect Mail Activity option. Apple recommends Block All Remote Content in that case. Keep Hide IP Address selected too, since Apple recommends that as well.
Next steps after you turn it on

Check the three options once, then leave them alone unless something breaks. Most of the work after that is about the mail itself. If one sender keeps filling your inbox, [block that sender](/how-to/block-a-sender-in-apple-mail). If a newsletter is the problem, [unsubscribe from the mailing list](/how-to/unsubscribe-from-a-mailing-list-in-apple-mail) instead of relying on privacy settings.
Privacy settings protect what your Mac shares. They don't clean up a crowded inbox. Those two jobs need different tools, and this setting only handles the first one.

faq.question: Is Mail Privacy Protection the same as Protect Mail Activity?
faq.answer: In practice, yes. Apple's help page title says Mail Privacy Protection. The option you select in Mail > Settings > Privacy is labeled Protect Mail Activity.

faq.question: Does Mail Privacy Protection block all email tracking?
faq.answer: No. Apple describes two effects: hiding your IP address from senders and downloading remote content in the background. Apple doesn't say it blocks every tracker. For stricter control, use Block All Remote Content.

faq.question: Do I need to turn on Hide IP Address separately?
faq.answer: Usually not. Apple selects Hide IP Address automatically when Protect Mail Activity is on. Make sure it stays selected, and keep it selected even if you turn Protect Mail Activity off.

faq.question: Why does Mail say my IP address isn't hidden?
faq.answer: Apple says your IP address isn't hidden on Wi-Fi or Ethernet when the network setting that limits IP address tracking is off. Turn that setting on for your connection, then check the Privacy pane again.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for this setting?
faq.answer: Not that Apple lists. The Apple Mail privacy pages I checked show no shortcut for this setting. Use the menu path Mail > Settings > Privacy.

faq.question: Can I turn on Mail Privacy Protection on iCloud.com?
faq.answer: Yes, under Privacy & Security in the iCloud.com Mail settings. Apple says the feature is not available in all countries or regions, so the option may be missing where you live.

faq.question: Does macOS 27 Golden Gate change these steps?
faq.answer: I found no change to the privacy setting in Apple's Mail What's new page. Apple's macOS 27 page showed beta-style wording when I checked, so confirm the labels on your own screen.

task: Turn on Mail Privacy Protection in Apple Mail on Mac
appliesTo: Apple Mail on Mac. Menu paths follow Apple's Mail help, which names no macOS version.
requirements: Apple Mail on your Mac, with at least one email account set up
Mail open and in front, so the Mail menu appears in the menu bar
iCloud.com in a browser, only if you want the web steps

steps.name: Open Apple Mail
steps.text: Open Mail from the Dock or from the Applications folder. Make sure Mail is the active app, with its name bold in the menu bar at the top of the screen. Click a Mail window if another app is in front.
steps.tip: The Mail menu only appears when Mail is the front app.

steps.name: Choose Mail > Settings
steps.text: Click Mail in the menu bar, then choose Settings. The Settings window opens. This is the Settings inside the Mail menu, not the System Settings app.
steps.tip: Apple writes this path as Mail > Settings. Don't confuse it with System Settings.

steps.name: Click Privacy
steps.text: In the Settings window, click Privacy. This pane holds the options for hiding your IP address and controlling remote content.
steps.tip: Keep this window open. The next steps all happen in this pane.

steps.name: Select Protect Mail Activity
steps.text: Select Protect Mail Activity. Apple says that when it is selected, your IP address is hidden from senders and remote content downloads in the background.
steps.tip: Apple's page title calls the feature Mail Privacy Protection. The option you select is labeled Protect Mail Activity.

steps.name: Check that Hide IP Address is selected
steps.text: Look for Hide IP Address in the same pane. Apple says it is selected automatically when Protect Mail Activity is on. Make sure it is still selected.
steps.tip: Keep it selected even if you later turn Protect Mail Activity off. Apple recommends that.

steps.name: Check the network setting for your connection
steps.text: Apple says that if the network setting that limits IP address tracking is off for Wi-Fi or Ethernet, your IP address is not hidden on that network. Apple doesn't give the exact menu path, so check the details for the connection you use.
steps.tip: The Apple Community thread calls this setting Limit IP Address Tracking. Use that name when you search.

steps.name: Close the Settings window
steps.text: Close the Settings window when you finish. The Apple pages I checked describe no separate save step for these options.
steps.tip: Send yourself a test message if you want to see how remote content loads for you.

troubleshooting.problem: Error: Your network preferences prevent content from loading privately
troubleshooting.fix: Check the Limit IP Address Tracking setting for your current Wi-Fi or Ethernet connection. Apple says IP addresses aren't hidden on a network where that setting is off. A 2021 community thread also suggests unchecking Auto Proxy Discovery and turning off third-party antivirus web shields. Those weaken other protection, so change one thing at a time.

troubleshooting.problem: IP address still visible on Wi-Fi or Ethernet
troubleshooting.fix: Apple says your IP address isn't hidden on a network where the Limit IP address tracking setting is off. Turn that setting on for the connection you use, then check that Hide IP Address is still selected.

troubleshooting.problem: Can't find Protect Mail Activity on iCloud.com
troubleshooting.fix: Go to Settings > Privacy & Security in the iCloud.com Mail settings. Apple says the feature isn't available in all countries or regions, so your region may not offer it.

troubleshooting.problem: Hide IP Address is off after you turned off Protect Mail Activity
troubleshooting.fix: Apple recommends keeping Hide IP Address selected even when Protect Mail Activity is off. Select it again in the Privacy pane.
